p: The king is Ptolemy IV of Egypt, who won at Raphia in 217 BC; his Greek surname means "father-loving."
b: Ptolemy IV, called Philopator ("lover of his father"), was king of Egypt; C. W. Emmet (1913) dates his reign 222-204 BC. His rival Antiochus is Antiochus III "the Great," who had taken Seleucia and occupied Syria and Palestine (Emmet, citing Polybius 5.40 and following). The book starts abruptly: its first Greek words are "Now Philopator," as if something came before, and 2:25 speaks of companions "already mentioned" whom the book never mentions. Ewald, Fritzsche and Grimm thought the opening was lost; Emmet thought the writer was copying a source carelessly (see the note on 2:25). Emmet takes Daniel 11:11-12 to refer to Raphia. There the "king of the south" wins, and "his heart will swell with pride" (Daniel 11:12).

p: Polybius, a Greek historian of the 100s BC, tells of the same battle near Gaza, fought in 217 BC.
b: Raphia lay near Gaza: after the battle Antiochus fell back into Raphia and the next day went on to Gaza (Polybius, Histories 5.86). Polybius describes the campaign at length (5.79-86). He says Ptolemy won with his phalanx, that Antiochus lost nearly ten thousand foot soldiers killed and more than four thousand taken prisoner, and that afterward the towns of Coele-Syria competed to honor the winner with crowns, sacrifices and altars (5.86). C. W. Emmet (1913) dates the battle to the spring of 217 BC and finds the book's account in substantial agreement with Polybius, with some differences of detail. Victor Tcherikover (1945) thought 1:1-7 came from historical sources of Philopator's reign.

p: Arsinoe was Ptolemy's sister at the time of Raphia; later she also became his wife.
b: The book calls Arsinoe only "his sister." C. W. Emmet (1913) notes that this was correct at the date of Raphia, and that afterward she became Ptolemy's wife, as Egyptian custom allowed (Livy calls her Cleopatra, Justin calls her Eurydice). Polybius says that before the battle the two kings rode along their lines to address the phalanx, Ptolemy supported by his sister Arsinoe among others (Histories 5.83). He does not describe her loosened hair or tears, or the promise of gold that 1:4 gives her; those details are the book's own, or come from a source now lost.

p: Polybius tells the same raid: Theodotus, a deserter from Ptolemy, missed the king and killed his doctor.
b: Theodotus had deserted Ptolemy and served Antiochus (Emmet, 1913, citing Polybius 5.40, 46 and 61). Polybius tells the raid in 5.81: Theodotus took two men with him, but the king used to sleep outside his main official tent, so Theodotus wounded two of those who slept there, killed the king's physician Andreas, and got away. Polybius blames him for not finding out where the king slept. 3 Maccabees tells it differently. It gives Theodotus "the finest Ptolemaic soldiers" (1:2; the Greek can also mean the best Ptolemaic arms, as Emmet notes), not two companions. It also says the king was saved because a Jew, Dositheus, moved him and put a stand-in in his bed (1:3). Emmet wondered whether that nobody is Polybius's Andreas. Both accounts agree that the king was not where the killer looked.

p: The man who saves the king's life is a Jew who has given up the law. The book makes nothing of his help.
b: Dositheus, "called Drimylus's son," is a Jew by birth who "changed the customs" (Greek metabalōn ta nomima) and became estranged from "the teachings of his fathers." In this book he appears only here, and Polybius, telling the same night raid, does not name him. C. W. Emmet (1913) reports that a Dositheus son of Drimylus is named as a priest of Alexander in 222 BC in a papyrus (Hibeh Papyrus 90), and that Josephus names a Dositheus as a Jewish general of a later Ptolemy. Emmet thought the writer joined the two and made the son of Drimylus a renegade Jew who saves the king, as Mordecai does in Esther (Esther 2:21-23). The writer marks him as an apostate and drops him. The book's later bargain, citizenship for those who give up the law (2:30-33), and the killing of apostates in 7:10-15, show how seriously it takes that line.

p: A mina was a hundred drachmas; two minas of gold for every man was a huge promise.
b: The mina was a Greek unit of weight and money, equal to a hundred drachmas (as NETS notes), and the Greek says these are minas of gold. C. W. Emmet (1913) called the promise "impossibly extravagant," but noted that Egyptian queens had large private property, and he reported Abrahams's suggestion that it was made only to the Greek mercenaries. Compare the reward of two thousand drachmas that the king offers informers in 3:28.

a: he handed out gifts to their shrines
p: Ptolemy honors the gods of the cities he has won; this sets up his visit to Jerusalem.
b: The Greek word is temenos, a sacred precinct around a temple. Polybius says the towns of Coele-Syria honored Ptolemy with crowns, sacrifices and altars after Raphia (Histories 5.86). C. W. Emmet (1913) points out the difference: Polybius stresses their gifts to the king, while 3 Maccabees stresses his gifts to them (1:6-7). Emmet adds that inscriptions show this king's ready liberality to cities and temples. So the king's visit to Jerusalem is meant to look like one more stop on a tour of thanks. In his own letter he boasts of it (3:16).

p: The gerousia, the council of elders of the Jews in Jerusalem.
b: Greek gerousia, from gerōn, "old man": a council of elders. In the letters of 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees the gerousia of the Jews writes or is written to, with the high priest or the people (1 Maccabees 12:6; 2 Maccabees 1:10; 2 Maccabees 11:27). Here the book adds "and from the elders," perhaps meaning the leading men of the city beyond the council.

t: A king at the sanctuary: 3 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees 3
p: The story of 1:8-2:24 runs close to the story of Heliodorus in 2 Maccabees 3. Here is how they compare.
b:
In 2 Maccabees 3 a Seleucid minister, Heliodorus, comes to take the temple treasure. The priests throw themselves down "in their priestly robes" (2 Maccabees 3:15), the unmarried girls "who were usually kept shut in" run out (2 Maccabees 3:19), the people pray, and God strikes him down: two young men "flogged him" until he fell and was carried out helpless (2 Maccabees 3:26-28). 3 Maccabees has every one of these steps (1:16-2:23), even the whipping (2:21).

The differences matter. Heliodorus wants money; Ptolemy wants to see the inner room. Heliodorus is saved by the high priest's sacrifice and confesses God (2 Maccabees 3:35-36); Ptolemy recovers and "felt no regret at all" (2:24), which drives the rest of the book. Which book depends on which is debated. C. W. Emmet (1913) wrote that it is "usually assumed without any serious attempt at proof" that 3 Maccabees used 2 Maccabees, and that Willrich argued the reverse; Emmet himself saw no direct borrowing either way, only two books of the same school and period.

p: The book keeps two words apart: hieron, the whole temple, and naos, the holy house the king wants to enter.
b: Hieron ("the temple") is the whole sacred complex with its courts, where Ptolemy has already sacrificed. Naos ("the sanctuary") is the holy building itself. The answer in 1:11 shows what the king is after: the room only the high priest enters once a year, the Most Holy Place behind the veil. The Gospels use the same two words, and it is "the curtain of the sanctuary" that splits in two (Matthew 27:51).

a: only the high priest, who leads them all, and he only one time each year
t: Once a year, the high priest alone
p: The rule of Leviticus 16, the Day of Atonement, also stated in Hebrews and, later, in the Mishnah.
b: Leviticus 16 allows Aaron into "the holy place behind the veil" only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:2, 34). Hebrews states the same rule: "The second tent, though, is entered by the high priest alone, once a year" (Hebrews 9:7). The Mishnah, compiled about AD 200, later than this book, ranks the zones of holiness: Gentiles may not pass the barrier around the inner courts, and "only the high priest, on Yom Kippur, at the time of the service" may enter the Holy of Holies (Mishnah Kelim 1:8-9). Ptolemy's demand breaks the strictest boundary in Israel's worship.
r: Leviticus 16:2; Leviticus 16:34; Hebrews 9:7; Numbers 18:7; Mishnah Kelim 1:8-9

t: Uzziah, the king who went in
p: Another king once forced his way into the sanctuary and was struck there: Uzziah of Judah.
b: 2 Chronicles tells how King Uzziah, once he was strong, "went into the LORD's temple to burn incense" (2 Chronicles 26:16). The priests told him, "it is not your place" (2 Chronicles 26:18), and as he raged, skin disease broke out on his forehead and "the LORD had struck him" (2 Chronicles 26:20). Both stories have the same shape: a proud king, priests who read him the rule, and a blow from God in the holy place itself. 3 Maccabees does not name Uzziah, but Jewish readers knew the pattern.

a: to boast about that very thing
p: The Greek verb means to tell of marvels or put on a show; the exact point of the reply is unclear.
b: Terateuesthai comes from teras, "wonder, portent." It can mean to talk of marvels, to boast, or to make a show of something. The Plain takes it as "boast," as Brenton (1851) and C. W. Emmet (1913) do (Brenton: "That he did wrong to boast of this"): the king should not boast of having entered other temples. It may instead mean that it was wrong to make a wonder of it. "Rashly" suggests the speaker was unwise to answer the king at all.

p: The book's favorite title for God, a Greek superlative also found in 2 Maccabees.
b: Ho megistos theos, literally "the greatest God," is the book's stock name for the God of Israel (here; 3:11, and often in chapters 4-7). The title claims for Israel's God the top place, in the Greek of the nations. 2 Maccabees uses it when Heliodorus reports "the works of the greatest God" (2 Maccabees 3:36). At 1:9 Codex Venetus has it where Alexandrinus says "the faithful God" (see the variant there), and here Venetus has "the great God."

a: Unmarried girls, who were kept shut in their rooms
p: Unmarried girls were kept at home; that they run into the street shows the panic.
b: Greek katakleistoi parthenoi, "virgins shut in." The writer takes it for granted that unmarried daughters stayed indoors and out of public view (compare Sirach 42:11, which tells a father to keep strict watch over a headstrong daughter). 2 Maccabees uses the same picture for Heliodorus's visit: "the unmarried girls, who were usually kept shut in" ran to the gates and walls (2 Maccabees 3:19). Both writers use the broken custom to show a city turned upside down.

p: Throwing dust on the head was a sign of grief and pleading, as in Joshua and Lamentations.
b: When Israel was beaten at Ai, Joshua and the elders "threw dust on their heads" (Joshua 7:6). In Lamentations, after Jerusalem fell, "Dust is on their heads; sackcloth is tied around them" (Lamentations 2:10). The gesture says: we are brought low to the ground, have pity on us. Here it is done before the disaster, as a plea to stop it.

p: A rare, piled-up Greek word: "the all-highest temple."
b: Panypertatos joins "all" (pan-), "over" (hyper) and a superlative ending: "above everything, highest of all." Brenton rendered it "the Most High temple." The writer loves such inflated words, the style of Greek rhetoric of his day; the Plain keeps the sense in simpler words.

a: They shouted that everyone should take up weapons
p: Some young men want to fight, but the elders bring them back to prayer. The book sides with the elders.
b: In 1 Maccabees, zeal for the law leads to armed revolt (1 Maccabees 2:27-28), and the Hasmoneans decide to fight even on the Sabbath (1 Maccabees 2:41). 3 Maccabees tells a different story: the bold citizens who call for arms are "turned back" to prayer, and it is prayer, not swords, that saves the temple (2:21). The same is true later in Egypt, where the Jews have no army and are saved by Eleazar's prayer (6:1-15). C. W. Emmet (1913) found in the book "an absolute faith in the power of prayer." Victor Tcherikover (1945) put it in the setting of his Roman date: with the king himself leading the persecution, the Jews could rely on nothing but trust in God.

p: The narrator writes as a Jew: "our people." And even the king's own men pray to Israel's God.
b: Greek syn tois hēmeterois, "with ours." The writer speaks as one of the Jewish community and assumes Jewish readers. The scene is striking: the king's Greek officers join the Jews in calling on "the one who holds every power." Jonah's sailors do the same when the storm hits (Jonah 1:14). In this book the Gentiles who matter are sometimes friends (3:8-10), not only enemies.

a: the walls and the whole floor echoed too
p: Creation itself seems to protest: the walls and floor join the cry.
b: The image of stones and walls that cry out appears in Habakkuk: "For the stone in the wall cries out, / and the wooden beam answers it" (Habakkuk 2:11). Jesus uses it at his entry to Jerusalem: "if these fall silent, the stones will shout it out" (Luke 19:40). The writer says only that it "seemed" so, but the effect is that the temple building itself refuses the outrage.

p: C. W. Emmet (1913) identifies him as Simon II, perhaps the high priest praised in Sirach 50.
b: C. W. Emmet (1913) identifies him as Simon II, son of Onias II, high priest about 219-199 BC, and thinks he may be the Simon praised in Sirach: "Simon son of Onias, the high priest, / mended the house while he lived" (Sirach 50:1). Emmet adds that it is doubtful whether Simon the Just of Jewish tradition is Simon I or Simon II. The Talmud tells how the high priest Shimon HaTzaddik (Simon the Righteous) put on the priestly vestments and went out to meet Alexander the Macedonian, who bowed before him and spared the temple (Bavli Yoma 69a).

p: Simon prays as Solomon did at the temple's dedication: on his knees, hands spread out.
b: When Solomon dedicated the temple he "lifted his open palms to the heavens" (1 Kings 8:22) and prayed "down on his knees, with his palms spread toward the heavens" (1 Kings 8:54). Simon's prayer that follows leans on Solomon's: God chose this place for his name and promised to hear prayer made there (2:9-10). Ezra prays the same way (Ezra 9:5).

a: Lord, Lord, King of the heavens and Master of all creation
p: Simon piles up titles for God, in the style of Greek-speaking Jewish prayer.
b: Each title has a Greek word behind it: Kyrie "Lord" (the Greek books have no divine name, so not "the LORD"), basileu tōn ouranōn "King of the heavens," despota "Master," hagie en hagiois "Holy One among the holy," monarche "only Ruler," and pantokratōr "Almighty." C. W. Emmet (1913) calls such a heaping up of God's titles a feature of Greek-speaking Jewish prayer, and compares the prayer of 2 Maccabees 1:24-25. He notes that monarchos is used of God nowhere else in the Septuagint. The titles do work: a God who rules all creation can rule one proud king.
orig: Κύριε, Κύριε, βασιλεῦ τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ δέσποτα πάσης τῆς κτίσεως

p: The Greek verb is used of a spirited horse; Psalm 2 uses it of the nations that rage against God.
b: The Greek pephryasmenou comes from phryassomai, to snort and toss the head like a spirited horse, and so to be haughty; the Plain says "puffed up." The Greek of Psalm 2:1 uses the same verb: "Why did the nations rage" (Acts 4:25, where the church quotes it under persecution). Simon's choice of word sets Ptolemy among the rulers of Psalm 2 who rise against the Lord.

p: Following the Greek of Genesis 6:4, Simon blames the giants for the wrong that brought the Flood.
b: Where the Hebrew of Genesis 6:4 has "the Nephilim," the Septuagint says gigantes, "giants." Jewish writers of this period told much of them: 1 Enoch says the Watchers' wives "gave birth to huge giants" (1 Enoch 7:2). A similar list of warnings, the giants, Lot's neighbors, and the six hundred thousand who hardened their hearts in the wilderness, appears in the Greek of Sirach 16:7-10, and Wisdom remembers the Flood "when the proud giants were dying" (Wisdom 14:6). Genesis itself blames human violence in general (Genesis 6:11-13). C. W. Emmet (1913) gathers these same passages beside this verse (with Judith 16:7 and Jubilees). Simon's prayer joins a Jewish way of reading Genesis that many books of the period share.
r: Genesis 6:4; Genesis 6:11-13; Sirach 16:7-10; Wisdom 14:6; 1 Enoch 7:1-6; 2 Peter 2:4-5

p: Simon names Sodom's sin as arrogance, as Ezekiel does; other passages stress violence and sexual sin.
b: Genesis 19 tells of the men of Sodom who tried to rape Lot's guests. Ezekiel names the root: "Here is the guilt of Sodom, your sister: pride" (Ezekiel 16:49). Jude stresses that they "went after other flesh" (Jude 7). Simon's prayer picks pride because the prayer is about a proud king: the idea comes back, in other Greek words, in 2:3, 2:17 and 2:21. Like 2 Peter, it makes Sodom a lesson: God set them "up as an example for those who would be ungodly later" (2 Peter 2:6).

a: you drowned him under the deep sea
p: Simon retells the crossing of the Sea of Reeds from Exodus 14-15.
b: In Exodus, "The waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, all Pharaoh's army" (Exodus 14:28), and then "Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD" (Exodus 15:1), as 2:8 says: "they praised you." Pharaoh's "testing" with plagues (2:6) and his drowning give the pattern for the whole book: a king who enslaves God's people, a rescue, and a song. In 6:4 the priest Eleazar will use the same example.

p: Simon builds on Deuteronomy's "place the LORD will choose" and Solomon's prayer.
b: Deuteronomy tells Israel to seek "the place the LORD your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name there" (Deuteronomy 12:5). Solomon's dedication prayer asks God to keep his eyes on the house where he said, "My name will be there" (1 Kings 8:29). Simon adds a Greek thought: God "needs nothing" (aprosdeēs; used of God, C. W. Emmet finds it in the Septuagint only here and in 2 Maccabees 14:35). A later Jewish prayer says the same: "You, Lord of all things, who lack nothing, chose with pleasure to have a temple" (2 Maccabees 14:35), and Paul tells the Athenians that God is not served "as if he were short of anything" (Acts 17:25).

p: Epiphaneia: a visible showing of God's power, the favorite word of 2 Maccabees.
b: Epiphaneia means an appearance or manifestation, especially a god's visible help. Here it recalls the glory that filled Solomon's temple at its dedication (1 Kings 8:10-11; 2 Chronicles 7:1-3). 2 Maccabees uses the word for God's interventions (2 Maccabees 3:24), and 3 Maccabees uses the noun again for the rescue at the hippodrome (5:8, 51), and the verb in 6:9 and 6:18. The same word gave the Christian feast of Epiphany its name.

p: Simon reminds God of the promise in Solomon's prayer: when Israel turns back and prays at the temple, God will hear.
b: Solomon asked: if the people sin and are defeated, then turn back and pray "in this house," hear and forgive (1 Kings 8:33-34). God answered that if his people humble themselves and pray, "I myself will hear from the heavens" (2 Chronicles 7:14). King Jehoshaphat used the promise in a crisis: "Out of our trouble we will cry to you, and you will hear and save" (2 Chronicles 20:9). Simon does the same. The Bible's words are a request in Solomon's mouth; Simon takes them as a promise.

p: The pair of words describes God in Deuteronomy's Greek and Christ in Revelation.
b: The Greek of Deuteronomy 32:4 calls God "faithful" (pistos) and his works "true" (alēthina). Revelation gives the pair to Christ as a name: "The one riding it is called Faithful and True" (Revelation 19:11; compare Revelation 3:14). Here it is the ground of the prayer: God will keep the promise just recalled.

a: because of our many great sins
p: Simon confesses the people's sins, although the outrage is the king's, not theirs.
b: The prayer follows the pattern of Israel's prayers after the exile: we have sinned, so we are under our enemies (Nehemiah 9:33-37; Daniel 9:5-16). In this story, though, the Jews have done nothing wrong; the book stresses their loyalty (3:3-5). Some readers see a humble confession that all Israel needs mercy; others see a tension in the book between this old explanation of suffering and its newer picture of innocent people persecuted for their faith, closer to Daniel 3 and 6. 2 Maccabees holds both together: the punishments are "meant, not for ruin, but for the correction of our people" (2 Maccabees 6:12).

p: The phrase comes from Solomon's prayer in the Greek: God's home is beyond all heavens, yet he chose a house on earth.
b: In the Greek of 1 Kings 8:27 Solomon says that "the heaven and the heaven of heaven" cannot hold God (the site's Plain, from the Hebrew: "the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you"). Simon makes the same two-sided point in 2:15-16: God lives where no human can reach, yet he chose to put his glory in this place. That is why its profaning matters. Isaiah 66:1 asks the question from the other side: "Where then is the house that you would build for me?"

a: Do not punish us through these men's uncleanness
p: The Greek "in" could mean "by means of" these men, or "for" their uncleanness. The first fits best.
b: The Greek preposition en can mean "in, by means of" or loosely "because of." Simon is not asking God to excuse Israel for the Gentiles' sin. He asks God not to use these unclean men as his tool to punish his people, as Habakkuk complained that God used the Babylonians (Habakkuk 1:12-13). Brenton has "by means of."
orig: μὴ ἐκδικήσῃς ἡμᾶς ἐν τῇ τούτων ἀκαθαρσίᾳ

a: We have trampled the house of holiness
p: The boast Simon fears is a lament heard often in Israel's Scriptures: the foe tramples the holy place.
b: Isaiah laments, "our foes have trampled your sanctuary" (Isaiah 63:18). Daniel's vision asks how long the holy place will be "trampled" (Daniel 8:13), and 1 Maccabees mourns, "Your holy place is trampled and profaned" (1 Maccabees 3:51). Jesus speaks of Jerusalem "trampled" by the nations (Luke 21:24), and Revelation of the holy city trampled for forty-two months (Revelation 11:2). The "loathsome idols" are prosochthismata, a Septuagint word for idols as things God loathes.

p: The verb of David's prayer in Psalm 51, in the Greek: wipe sins away like writing from a page.
b: Apaleiphō means to wipe off, as ink from a page. Psalm 51 asks God to "wipe out my rebellions" (Psalm 51:1), and Isaiah hears God say, "I myself, I am the one / who wipes away your rebellions" (Isaiah 43:25). Simon prays in the words of Israel's own Scripture.

p: Simon quotes the Greek of Psalm 79:8, a lament over a temple defiled by the nations.
b: The Greek words are those of Psalm 78:8 in the Septuagint (Psalm 79:8 in English Bibles): tachy prokatalabetōsan hēmas hoi oiktirmoi sou. (Swete's text of 3 Maccabees lacks hēmas, "us"; see the variant.) The site's Plain renders that verse from the Hebrew: "Hurry, let your compassion come out to meet us" (Psalm 79:8). The choice is apt, for Psalm 79 begins: "God, the nations have come in, into your inheritance. / They have made your holy temple unclean" (Psalm 79:1). The closing words echo Psalm 34:18: "he saves those whose spirits are crushed."

p: A rare title for God: propatōr, "forefather." Paul uses the word of Abraham.
b: Propatōr means a first ancestor. Paul uses it of Abraham, "our forefather according to the flesh" (Romans 4:1). C. W. Emmet (1913) lists it among titles of God found nowhere else in the Septuagint. Calling God the forefather of Israel is unusual; it may mean the first Father of all things, or the Father of the nation (compare Deuteronomy 32:6; Isaiah 63:16). Brenton found the phrase hard and wrote "who is beyond all Holy among the holy." The prayer is called enthesmos, "lawful": offered as it should be, by the right person in the right place.

p: The answer to prayer is a blow from God, as with Heliodorus and later Herod. The 66 books tell such stories too.
b: Heliodorus was "flogged from heaven" (2 Maccabees 3:34) by two young men; here God himself does the whipping, with no angel named. The 66 books have their own stories of proud rulers struck by God: Uzziah in the temple (2 Chronicles 26:20), Nebuchadnezzar driven out to the fields (Daniel 4:31-33), and Herod Agrippa, whom "an angel of the Lord struck" because he took God's glory (Acts 12:23). 3 Maccabees agrees with them that God defends his honor; it goes beyond them in telling of such a blow to a king of Egypt.

a: as the wind tosses a reed
p: The image of weakness Jesus later uses of the people's expectations about John the Baptist.
b: A reed bends whichever way the wind pushes it. Jesus asks the crowds about John: "what did you go to gaze at? A reed that the wind shakes?" (Matthew 11:7). Here the mighty king is the reed, shaken this way and that by God. Compare the bruised reed of Isaiah 42:3, which God's servant will not break.

p: "Friend" is a title at the king's court, as in 1 and 2 Maccabees.
b: The philoi, "Friends," are the king's inner circle. The site writes it with a capital, as in 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees ("one of the king's Friends"). At 2:26 many of these Friends follow the king's will against the Jews.

a: he felt no regret at all
t: A heart that does not change
p: Unlike Heliodorus, Ptolemy learns nothing. His hardness drives the rest of the book.
b: Heliodorus, once struck, sacrifices to God and tells everyone of his power (2 Maccabees 3:35-36). Ptolemy goes home "making bitter threats." Compare Pharaoh, who, when the hail stopped, "sinned once more. He made his heart heavy" (Exodus 9:34). He changes only later, after God puts "a forgetting" into his mind (5:28) and at last turns his anger into pity (6:22). The Greek metamelos means "regret, change of mind"; Matthew uses the related verb when Judas "regretted it" (Matthew 27:3).

p: No drinking companions have been mentioned in the book as we have it.
b: The Greek proapodedeigmenōn means "previously pointed out" or "appointed before." The book has not named any drinking partners. C. W. Emmet (1913) gives two explanations: a slip by a writer copying a source carelessly, or a sign that the book's opening has been lost (see the note on 1:1). The king's drinking returns in chapter 5 (5:16).

a: ugly talk sprang up in those places
p: Dysphēmia means words of ill omen: slander, or even blasphemy.
b: Dysphēmia is the opposite of euphēmia, holy silence or speaking well. It can mean slander of people or blasphemy against the gods. "In those places" is vague: in Egypt, perhaps in the Jews' own places of prayer. Brenton has "he raised evil reports there"; C. W. Emmet (1913) adds that it is not clear whether the reports were against the king himself or against the Jews. The verse explains the next one: the talk prepares a public decree.

a: he put up a stone pillar
p: Ptolemaic inscriptions speak of records set up on stone; the book has the king set up his at the court.
b: A stēlē was an upright stone slab carved with a text. C. W. Emmet (1913) notes that the Canopus and Rosetta inscriptions of the Ptolemaic age speak of records set up on a stēlē, and use the same verb for enrolling that 2:29 uses. Esther shows the same practice in Persia: a copy of the order "was to be given out as law in each province and shown openly to all the peoples" (Esther 8:13). "The tower beside the palace courtyard" puts the pillar at the royal court.

a: No one who does not sacrifice may enter their temples
p: "Their" may mean the Jews' own places of worship, or the temples of Alexandria.
b: Greek epi ta hiera autōn, "into their sacred places." If "their" means the Jews, the decree bars from the Jews' own houses of prayer anyone who will not sacrifice to the king's gods; Brenton takes it so ("their own temple"). C. W. Emmet (1913) read it so too: the Jews might keep their own worship only if they also joined the official cult. If it means the pagan temples, the decree simply makes sacrifice the price of public religious life. Either way it forces a choice between the city's gods and Israel's God, as Daniel 3 did with the golden statue.
orig: ἐπὶ τὰ ἱερὰ αὐτῶν (epi ta hiera autōn)

p: A list of people for taxes, mostly native Egyptians; being on it set you among the common people.
b: Laographia, literally "people-writing," is a register of people. C. W. Emmet (1913) reports that Grenfell and Hunt found the word in Ptolemaic papyri, meaning "a taxing list of persons, most, or all, of whom were native Egyptians," and that laos was the technical word for Egyptians as against Greeks. Brenton has "registered among the common people." Here the list is joined to "the condition of household slaves," so the writer treats being listed as a loss of standing. Victor Tcherikover (1945) noted that the word meant a census of the people at the end of the Ptolemaic period and a poll tax in the Roman period, and he read this verse against the census under Augustus that listed those who paid the poll tax. Luke's "the whole inhabited world was to be registered" (Luke 2:1) uses the related verb apographō, as 2:29 and 2:32 do.

p: Dionysus was the family god of the Ptolemies; the ivy was his plant.
b: Ivy was sacred to Dionysus (Bacchus), and his worshipers carried it, as in 2 Maccabees: "they were made to march in Dionysus's parade carrying ivy" (2 Maccabees 6:7). C. W. Emmet (1913) notes good evidence that Dionysus was the family god of the Ptolemies, and an entry in a later Greek dictionary saying that Ptolemy Philopator was called Gallos because he was tattooed with ivy leaves like the Galli. If that report is right, the king orders for the Jews the mark he is said to have worn himself.

p: The law forbade marks on the skin; Revelation's "mark" is a word from the same root as the verb here.
b: The verb is charassesthai, "to be engraved, branded." The noun from the same root, charagma, is the "mark" of the beast that everyone must take "on their right hand or on their forehead" (Revelation 13:16). Slaves were branded to show who owned them, as the Cambridge Bible notes on Revelation 13:16, so the mark also says "owned." The law of Moses forbade it: "do not put tattooed writing on yourselves. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:28). Paul, by contrast, says he carries "the marks of Jesus" in his body (Galatians 6:17), using another word.

a: under the reduced rights already set for them
p: A hard phrase: perhaps the lower legal standing set out earlier for the Jews.
b: The Greek eis tēn prosynestalmenēn authentian is obscure: authentia means "authority" or "status," and the participle means "restricted beforehand." It seems to mean that the registered Jews would be entered on the rolls with the lesser standing already decreed in 2:28. Brenton has "set apart with these limited rights." The verb, katachōrizō, "enter in a register," is a technical word of the papyri, C. W. Emmet (1913) notes; on the readings with and without "beforehand," see the variant on this verse.
orig: οὓς καὶ προκαταχωρίσαι εἰς τὴν προσυνεσταλμένην αὐθεντίαν

p: Jews who join the mysteries of Dionysus may become equal citizens. The offer is the book's real test.
b: Teletai were initiation rites; here, those of the mysteries of Dionysus, whose ivy the decree has just named (2:29). The king offers what Alexandrian Jews were seeking, equal standing with the Greek citizens of the city, at the price of their faith. Victor Tcherikover (1945) read the book as treating the Jews' pursuit of civic rights in Alexandria as "nothing short of a betrayal of Jewish interests." For the writer, a Jew who buys citizenship this way has left the people of God (2:33).
orig: ἐν τοῖς κατὰ τελετὰς μεμυημένοις (en tois kata teletas memyēmenois)

p: Isopolitai: people with the same civic rights. The Jews' legal standing in Alexandria was a burning question.
b: Isopolitēs means one who has equal citizen rights. C. W. Emmet (1913) calls the question of Alexandrian citizenship "complicated": Josephus says more than once that the Jews already had full citizenship, but Emmet thought that whatever rights they had at this period they held as individuals and not as a nation. The book's view is plain: citizenship is good when offered fairly (3:21, where the king boasts of offering it), but not at the cost of the law. The word politeia, "citizenship" (3:21, 23), is the same word that 2 Maccabees uses for a people's lawful "ways of life" (2 Maccabees 4:11).

a: the price that the city's godliness asked of them
p: A hard phrase. Epibathra means a step, a gangplank or a fare; the sense seems to be the cost of faithfulness.
b: Literally "hating the epibathra of the city's godliness" (tas tēs poleōs eusebeias epibathras). Epibathra is a step up or a boarding plank, and also the fare paid to board. C. W. Emmet (1913) took it as "the price paid," thinking of the heavy demands of the law, or of the temple tax. The Greek says only "the city"; it does not say which. For "lightly" Venetus first wrote "over the city" (see the variant), and Brenton has "those who were over the city." Whichever is right, the point is clear: some Jews found their faith a burden and traded it for status.

a: They loathed those of their own who went over
p: The faithful cut off those who went over to the king. The book returns to them at its end.
b: The faithful Jews treat the converts as "enemies of the nation" and shut them out of shared life and mutual help. The book approves, and at the end it has the king allow the faithful to kill such apostates (7:10-15, see the notes there). The Bible itself has rules for excluding the unfaithful from the community (Ezra 10:8; 1 Corinthians 5:11), but the line from exclusion to violence is the hard question this book raises.

a: the Jews out in the country
p: The book sets the Jews of Alexandria beside those of the countryside, the chōra.
b: Greek tois en tē chōra, "those in the country." The verse sets them beside the Jews of Alexandria: the king's anger now spreads from the capital to every Jew in the land, as in Esther the decree goes "to every province of the king" (Esther 3:13). C. W. Emmet (1913) thought probable Büchler's view that the persecution behind the story fell on Jews of the Fayum, a district of the countryside, who were brought to Alexandria.
orig: τοῖς ἐν τῇ χώρᾳ (tois en tē chōra)

a: the Jews kept them from their customs
t: What were the Jews accused of?
p: The charge is hard to pin down in the Greek: perhaps that Jews hindered others' customs, or kept apart from them.
b: The Greek hōs an apo tōn nomimōn autous kōlyontōn says "as if they were hindering them from the customs." It may mean the Jews were blamed for keeping others from the city's religious customs, or for standing in the way of the king's laws. Brenton has "the Jews kept them away from the ordinances of the law." Verses 4-7 make the real issue clear: Jewish separateness in worship and food.
orig: ὡς ἂν ἀπὸ τῶν νομίμων αὐτοὺς κωλυόντων

p: The food laws set the Jews apart, and their neighbors resented it, as Haman says in Esther.
b: The laws of clean and unclean food (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14) meant that Jews could not share most pagan meals or sacrifices. Daniel "set his heart on not defiling himself with the king's rich food" (Daniel 1:8). Haman's charge to the Persian king is the same as here: "Their laws are unlike any other people's, and the king's laws they do not obey" (Esther 3:8). The writer admits the separation and defends it: they kept apart in food, but were just and well liked in everything else (3:5).

p: Allophyloi: the book's word for the hostile non-Jews, set apart from the friendly "Greeks in the city" (3:8).
b: Allophyloi, "those of another tribe," is the Septuagint's word for the Philistines and for foreigners. The writer uses it of the enemies of the Jews in Egypt, but he is careful to add that "the Greeks in the city" had suffered no wrong and tried to help (3:8-10). Not all Gentiles are enemies in this book; the hostile ones are a group set on harm.

a: share the drink offerings of alliance
p: Greek homospondoi: people who pour a drink offering together when they make a treaty.
b: Treaties in the Greek world were sealed by pouring a libation to the gods together (spondē), so homospondos meant "ally." The accusation has two edges: the Jews are not loyal allies, and they will not join in the gods' rites that sealed every alliance. The book answers both: they are loyal (3:3), but they will not worship other gods.

p: The Greeks of Alexandria pity the Jews but dare not help; the writer calls the king's rule a tyranny.
b: In Greek political thought a tyrant was a ruler who governs by fear and for himself. The writer, who calls the king "impious" (3:1), puts that word on his rule. He also makes a point about his Greek neighbors: they knew the Jews had done no wrong, comforted them, and expected things to change. Some even pledged secret help (3:10). The Greek diathesis means "condition" or "state of affairs" (C. W. Emmet notes this sense in Polybius), so the phrase may mean "the situation was one of tyranny."

a: a community that large, guilty of nothing
p: Either an innocent community will not be neglected, or "the One who knows everything" will not neglect it.
b: Mēden ēgnoēkos can mean "having done nothing wrong" (agnoeō, "to sin unknowingly") or "having been ignorant of nothing." The Plain takes it with "community": a large, innocent people would not be left alone. Brenton took it of God: "He who knoweth all things, will not ... disregard so great a people." On that reading the Greeks of the city voice a hope in providence.
orig: μὴ γὰρ οὕτω παροραθήσεσθαι τηλικοῦτο σύστεμα μηδὲν ἠγνοηκός

a: he wrote the following letter aimed at them
p: The letter of 3:12-29 closely resembles the king's letter against the Jews in the Greek Esther (Addition B).
b: The Greek Esther includes the text of the Persian king's decree (Addition B, at Esther 3:13 on this site): one hostile people, scattered among the nations, follows strange laws and ignores royal orders, so all are to be destroyed with wives and children. Ptolemy's letter makes the same charges and orders the same fate (3:19, 25). In both books a second letter later reverses the first (Esther's Addition E at 8:12; 3 Maccabees 7:1-9), and a yearly feast follows. The two books may be drawing on each other or on a shared pattern.

p: Stratēgos first means "general"; in this book the stratēgoi run the cities and districts.
b: Stratēgos first means "general": C. W. Emmet (1913) translates "generals" here, and Brenton "commanders." In this book the stratēgoi carry out the king's orders in each city and district (4:4; 4:18; 6:41; 7:1), so the site renders the word "governors" throughout the book. The greeting "greetings and good health" (chairein kai errōsthai, as in 7:1) is a formula Emmet found in the Letter of Aristeas and in Egyptian papyri of about 100 BC; he used it to date the book. A wish for health follows (3:13), as in 2 Maccabees 9:19-20.

a: In word they welcomed our coming, but in deed they were false
p: The letter retells chapters 1-2 from the king's point of view, leaving out his own humiliation.
b: In the king's version he came only to honor the temple with gifts, was falsely welcomed, and spared the Jews out of kindness. He says nothing of being struck down. The reader, who has just seen it, knows the letter is self-serving, and the gap is the writer's irony. The same device runs through Esther, where Haman's words to the king hide what he intends (Esther 3:8-9).

p: The charge that the Jews stand against everyone; Haman makes it in Esther.
b: The letter accuses the Jews of being the only people who hold their heads high against kings. Haman's charge in Esther is similar (Esther 3:8), and the Greek Esther's royal letter calls them "one hostile people" among all nations. The writer lets the charge stand in the king's mouth, so that the reader can measure it against what he has already said: the Jews were loyal and well thought of by everyone (3:3-5). C. W. Emmet (1913) points to the Letter of Aristeas, which defends Jewish separateness in food and life (Aristeas 128 and following).

p: The king claims he offered the Jews full citizenship of Alexandria, the honor they most wanted.
b: The king boasts that he wanted to raise the Jews to politeia, the citizenship of the Greek city, and blames them for refusing. The reader knows the hidden price from 2:30: initiation into the king's cult. "Their kin here" are the Jews of Egypt, kin to those of Jerusalem. On "their service as allies," C. W. Emmet (1913) recalls that Jewish garrisons already guarded Egypt's southern border at Elephantine and Aswan under the Persians, in the 400s BC.

p: To a Greek king, a barbaros was anyone who did not speak Greek or live as a Greek.
b: Barbaros first meant someone whose speech sounds like "bar-bar," a non-Greek. The king calls Greek-speaking Jews of Alexandria "barbarians," denying them a place in Greek civilization. 2 Maccabees turns the word around, saying the Jewish fighters "drove the barbarian crowds before them" (2 Maccabees 2:21), and Paul uses it simply of non-Greek speakers (Romans 1:14).

p: The verb means to beat on the tympanon, a frame used for torture. Hebrews uses the same word of the martyrs.
b: Apotympanizō comes from tympanon, a drum, and also the torture frame of 2 Maccabees 6:19. Eleazar in 2 Maccabees "walked toward the torture frame" (2 Maccabees 6:19), and Hebrews remembers that "others were tortured on the rack" (Hebrews 11:35), with the verb tympanizō. The threat falls on any Gentile who hides a Jew, which is just what the friendly neighbors of 3:10 had promised to do.

t: From the old to the infant
p: The decree, like Haman's, spares no one, "from the young to the old, little children and women" (Esther 3:13).
b: Esther's decree orders the Jews killed "from the young to the old, little children and women, all in one day" (Esther 3:13). Ptolemy's letter goes further by threatening the Gentiles who shelter them. Pharaoh's order against Hebrew babies (Exodus 1:22) is the oldest pattern behind both.

p: A slave who informs will be freed. The decree in the Letter of Aristeas also pays informers.
b: "Crowned with freedom" seems to mean that the informer, if a slave, will be set free. C. W. Emmet (1913) reports that Deissmann found "crown" used in papyri for "reward," and that the formula "anyone who wishes may inform" is familiar in papyri; the royal decree in the Letter of Aristeas (25) also rewards informers. The informer also gets the property of the person he reports and two thousand drachmas (see 1:4 on money). The writer means the reader to feel how such a decree would turn neighbors and household servants against each other.

a: that place is to be put off-limits and set on fire
p: Persian decrees in Ezra and Daniel end with the same kind of threat against a guilty house.
b: Royal decrees in the Bible end with threats like this. Darius orders that a man who changes his decree be impaled and "His house is to be made a dunghill for this" (Ezra 6:11); Nebuchadnezzar says that anyone who speaks against Israel's God will be hacked apart "and its house will be made a dunghill" (Daniel 3:29). The Greek Esther's second royal letter ends with the same sort of threat against any city that disobeys. Here the threat is turned against those who protect the Jews.
